title: Linked lists
summary: Chain nodes together with references, then insert, remove and reverse by rewiring them.

steps.title: Nodes and next pointers
body: A **linked list** does not need one block of memory. Each item lives in its own **node**, which holds a value and a reference to the next node. The last node's `Next` is `null`.
To visit every item you start at `head` and follow `Next` until you fall off the end. Step through the trace and watch `cur` hop from node to node.

code: var head = new Node(1, new Node(2, new Node(3, null)));
public Node(int value, Node? next) { Value = value; Next = next; }

steps.prompt: Adding at the front just makes a new head. What does this print?
code: for (var cur = head; cur != null; cur = cur.Next)
public Node(int value, Node? next) { Value = value; Next = next; }
steps.explain: Each new node points at the old head and becomes the new head, so the list comes out in reverse order of insertion. Adding at the front is `O(1)`: nothing shifts.

steps.title: Insert and remove by rewiring
body: To insert after a node `prev`, point the new node at whatever came after `prev`, **then** point `prev` at the new node:
To remove the node after `prev`, skip over it: `prev.Next = prev.Next.Next;`. Nobody points at it any more, so the garbage collector reclaims it.
No shifting either way: both are `O(1)` once you are standing at `prev`. Getting there is the slow part, because there is no `list[i]` jump.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines to insert a new node holding `v` after `prev`, without losing the rest of the list.
steps.explain: If `prev.Next = node` ran first, the reference to the rest of the list would be overwritten before `node` could take it.

steps.prompt: Which operation is **slower** on a linked list than on an array?
options: Removing the node after one you already hold
steps.explain: An array jumps straight to index 500. A linked list has to follow 500 `Next` references: `O(n)`.

steps.title: Reversing in place
body: Reversing a linked list is a classic: walk once, turning each `Next` arrow around. You need three references:
- `next`: saved before flipping, so the rest of the list is not lost.
Watch the trace print the list before and after. Every arrow is flipped exactly once: `O(n)` time, `O(1)` space.

code: var head = new Node(1, new Node(2, new Node(3, null)));
for (var n = prev; n != null; n = n.Next) Console.Write(n.Value + " ");
public Node(int value, Node? next) { Value = value; Next = next; }

steps.explain: Save the rest, flip the arrow, then step both `prev` and `cur` forward. When `cur` is `null`, `prev` is the new head.

steps.title: Linked list toolkit
prompt: public Node(int value, Node? next) { Value = value; Next = next; }
Write three functions (do not declare `Node` yourself):
- `Node? Reverse(Node? head)`: reverse in place and return the new head.
- `Node? RemoveFirst(Node? head, int value)`: remove the **first** node holding `value` (if any) and return the head, which changes when the head itself is removed.
solution: for (var cur = head; cur != null; cur = cur.Next) n++;
while (prev.Next != null && prev.Next.Value != value) prev = prev.Next;
template: Node? DojoBuild(params int[] values) { Node? h = null; for (var i = values.Length - 1; i >= 0; i--) h = new Node(values[i], h); return h; }
string DojoShow(Node? h) { var parts = new List<string>(); for (var c = h; c != null; c = c.Next) parts.Add(c.Value.ToString()); return string.Join(",", parts); }
Dojo.Eq("Length of an empty list is 0", 0, Length(null));
Dojo.Eq("a missing value changes nothing", "1,2", DojoShow(RemoveFirst(DojoBuild(1, 2), 9)));
Dojo.Eq("remove from an empty list", "", DojoShow(RemoveFirst(null, 1)));
public Node(int value, Node? next) { Value = value; Next = next; }
hints: `Length`: `for (var cur = head; cur != null; cur = cur.Next) n++;`.
`Reverse`: the `prev` / `cur` / `next` loop from the card, returning `prev`.
`RemoveFirst`: handle `head.Value == value` first (return `head.Next`). Otherwise walk `prev` until `prev.Next` holds the value, then `prev.Next = prev.Next.Next`.
